mn39:1.2: On one occasion the Blessed One was living in the Angan country. There is a town of the Angans called Assapura.
mn39:1.3: There he addressed the bhikkhus thus:
mn39:2.1: ‘“Monks, Monks”, bhikkhus, that is how people perceive you.
mn39:2.2: And when you are asked “What are you?”, you claim that you are monks.
mn39:2.3: Since that is how you are reputed and how you claim, you should train thus: “We shall try to live up to such dhammas as constitute the Monk and as constitute the Divine, so that our reputations may be true and our claims represent what actually is,
mn39:2.4: and so that the acts of those whose robes, alms-food, resting-place and requisite of medicine as cure for the sick we use will furnish them great fruit and benefit in us, and so that our going forth shall not be in vain but fruitful and fertile.”
mn39:2.5: That is how you should train.
mn39:3.1: ‘What dhammas constitute the Monk and constitute the Divine?
mn39:3.2: You should train thus: “We shall be possessed of conscience and shame.”
mn39:3.3: Now, bhikkhus, it may be that you consider thus:
mn39:3.4: “We are possessed of conscience and shame: with that much it is enough, with that much it is done, the Monk’s goal has been reached and there is nothing more for us to do,” and that you rest content with that much.
mn39:3.5: Bhikkhus, I tell you, I declare to you:
mn39:3.6: You who seek the Monks’ status, do not fall short of the Monks’ goal, for there is more to be done.
mn39:4.2: You should train thus: “Our bodily conduct will be purified, frank and open, not inconsistent but restrained,
mn39:4.3: and we shall not laud ourselves and disparage others on account of that purified bodily conduct.”
mn39:4.4: Now, bhikkhus, it may be that you consider thus:
mn39:4.5: “We are possessed of conscience and shame, and we are purified in bodily conduct:
mn39:4.6: with that much it is enough, with that much it is done, the Monks’ goal has been reached and there is nothing more for us to do,” and that you rest content with that much.
mn39:4.7: Bhikkhus, I tell you, I declare to you:
mn39:4.8: You who seek the Monks’ status, do not fall short of the Monks’ goal, for there is more to be done.
mn39:5.2: You should train thus: “Our verbal conduct will be purified, frank and open, not inconsistent but restrained,
mn39:5.3: and we shall not laud ourselves and disparage others on account of that purified verbal conduct.”
mn39:5.4: Now, bhikkhus, it may be that you consider thus:
mn39:5.5: “We are possessed of conscience and shame, and we are purified in bodily conduct and verbal conduct:
mn39:5.6: with that much it is enough, with that much it is done, the Monks’ goal has been reached and there is nothing more for us to do,” and that you rest content with that much.
mn39:5.7: Bhikkhus, I tell you, I declare to you:
mn39:5.8: You who seek the Monks’ status, do not fall short of the Monks’ goal, for there is more to be done.
mn39:6.2: You should train thus: “Our mental conduct will be purified, frank and open, not inconsistent but restrained,
mn39:6.3: and we shall not laud ourselves and disparage others on account of that purified mental conduct.”
mn39:6.4: Now, bhikkhus, it may be that you consider thus:
mn39:6.5: “We are possessed of conscience and shame, and we are purified in bodily conduct, verbal conduct and mental conduct:
mn39:6.6: with that much it is enough, with that much it is done, the Monks’ goal has been reached and there is nothing more for us to do,” and that you rest content with that much.
mn39:6.7: Bhikkhus, I tell you, I declare to you:
mn39:6.8: You who seek the Monks’ status, do not fall short of the Monks’ goal, for there is more to be done.
mn39:7.2: You should train thus: “Our livelihood will be purified, frank and open, not inconsistent but restrained,
mn39:7.3: and we shall not laud ourselves and disparage others on account of that purified livelihood.”
mn39:7.4: Now, bhikkhus, it may be that you consider thus:
mn39:7.5: “We are possessed of conscience and shame, and we are purified in bodily conduct, verbal conduct, mental conduct and livelihood:
mn39:7.6: with that much it is enough, with that much it is done, the Monks’ goal has been reached and there is nothing more for us to do,” and that you rest content with that much.
mn39:7.7: Bhikkhus, I tell you, I declare to you:
mn39:7.8: You who seek the Monks’ status, do not fall short of the Monks’ goal, for there is more to be done.
mn39:8.2: You should train thus: “We shall keep the doors of the faculties guarded.
mn39:8.3: On seeing a form with the eye, we shall apprehend no signs and features
mn39:8.4: through which, if we leave the eye-door unguarded, evil unprofitable dhammas of covetousness and grief might invade us; we shall practise the way of its restraint, we shall guard the eye-faculty, undertake the restraint of the eye-faculty.
mn39:8.5: On hearing a sound with the ear …
mn39:8.6: On smelling an odour with the nose …
mn39:8.7: On tasting a flavour with the tongue …
mn39:8.8: On touching a tangible with the body …
mn39:8.9: On cognizing a dhamma with the mind, we shall apprehend no signs and features
mn39:8.10: which, if we leave the mind-door unguarded, evil unprofitable dhammas of covetousness and grief might invade us; we shall practise the way of its restraint, we shall guard the mind-faculty, undertake the restraint of the mind-faculty.”
mn39:8.11: Now, bhikkhus, it may be that you consider thus:
mn39:8.12: “We are possessed of conscience and shame, and we are purified in bodily conduct, verbal conduct and mental conduct, and we are guarded in the doors of our faculties:
mn39:8.13: with that much it is enough, with that much it is done, the Monks’ goal has been reached and there is nothing more for us to do,” and that you rest content with that much.
mn39:8.14: Bhikkhus, I tell you, I declare to you:
mn39:8.15: You who seek the Monks’ status, do not fall short of the Monks’ goal, for there is more to be done.
mn39:9.2: You should train thus: “We shall know the right amount in eating.
mn39:9.3: Reflecting wisely, we shall nourish ourselves with nutriment neither for amusement nor for intoxication (of vanity) nor for smartening nor for embellishment, but only for the endurance and continuance of this body, for the ending of discomfort, and for assisting the life divine, (considering:) ‘Thus I shall terminate old feelings without arousing new feelings and blameless shall live in comfort and health.’”
mn39:9.4: Now, bhikkhus, it may be that you consider thus:
mn39:9.5: “We are possessed of conscience and shame, we are purified in bodily conduct, verbal conduct, and mental conduct, we are guarded in the doors of our faculties, and we know the right amount in eating:
mn39:9.6: with that much it is enough, with that much it is done, the Monks’ goal has been reached and there is nothing more for us to do,” and that you rest content with that much.
mn39:9.7: Bhikkhus, I tell you, I declare to you:
mn39:9.8: You who seek the Monks’ status, do not fall short of the Monks’ goal, for there is more to be done.
mn39:10.2: You should train thus: “We shall be devoted to wakefulness. By day while walking and sitting[^1] we shall purify the mind of obstructive dhammas.
mn39:10.3: In the first watch of the night while walking and sitting we shall purify the mind of obstructive dhammas.
mn39:10.4: In the middle watch of the night we shall lie down on the right side in the lion’s sleeping pose with one foot overlapping the other, mindful and fully aware, after noting in our mind the time of rising.
mn39:10.5: After rising, in the third watch while walking and sitting we shall purify the mind of obstructive dhammas.”
mn39:10.6: Now, bhikkhus, it may be that you consider thus:
mn39:10.7: “We are possessed of conscience and shame, we are purified in bodily conduct, verbal conduct and mental conduct, we are guarded in the doors of our faculties, we know the right amount in eating, and we are devoted to wakefulness:
mn39:10.8: with that much it is enough, with that much it is done, the Monks’ goal has been reached and there is nothing more for us to do,” and that you rest content with that much.
mn39:10.9: Bhikkhus, I tell you, I declare to you:
mn39:10.10: You who seek the Monks’ status, do not fall short of the Monks’ goal, for there is more to be done.
mn39:11.2: You should train thus: “We shall be possessed of mindfulness and full awareness. We shall act in full awareness when moving forward and moving backward; we shall act in full awareness when looking towards and looking away; we shall act in full awareness when flexing and extending; we shall act in full awareness when wearing the patched cloak, bowl and robes; we shall act in full awareness when eating, drinking, chewing and tasting; we shall act in full awareness when evacuating the bowels and making water; we shall act in full awareness when walking, standing, sitting, falling asleep, waking up, talking and keeping silent.”
mn39:11.3: Now, bhikkhus, it may be that you consider thus:
mn39:11.4: “We are possessed of conscience and shame, we are purified in bodily, verbal and mental conduct, we are guarded in the doors of our faculties, we know the right amount in eating, we are devoted to wakefulness, and we are possessed of mindfulness and full awareness:
mn39:11.5: with that much it is enough, with that much it is done, the Monks’ goal has been reached and there is nothing more for us to do,” and that you rest content with that much.
mn39:11.6: Bhikkhus, I tell you, I declare to you:
mn39:11.7: You who seek the Monks’ status, do not fall short of the Monks’ goal, for there is more to be done.
mn39:12.2: Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu resorts to a secluded resting-place: to the forest, to the root of a tree, a rock, a hill-cleft, a mountain cave, a charnel ground, a woodland solitude, an open space, or a heap of straw.
mn39:13.1: On returning from his alms-round after his meal, he sits down; having folded his legs crosswise, sets his body erect, and establishes mindfulness before him.
mn39:13.2: Abandoning covetousness for the world, he abides with his mind free from covetousness, he purifies his mind of covetousness.
mn39:13.3: Abandoning ill-will and hatred, he abides with his mind free from ill-will; with pity for all creatures and beings, he purifies his mind of ill-will and hatred.
mn39:13.4: Abandoning lethargy and drowsiness, he abides free from lethargy and drowsiness, percipient of light, mindful and fully aware, he purifies his mind of lethargy and drowsiness.
mn39:13.5: Abandoning agitation and worry, he abides unagitated with a mind calmed in himself, he purifies his mind of agitation and worry.
mn39:13.6: Abandoning uncertainty, he abides with uncertainty crossed over, undoubting about profitable dhammas, he purifies his mind of uncertainty.
mn39:14.1: Suppose, bhikkhus, a man borrowed a loan and undertook works,
mn39:14.3: so that he repaid all the money of the old loan, and there remained over some extra for his wife and children.
mn39:14.4: Then it would occur to him:
mn39:14.5: ‘Formerly I borrowed a loan and undertook works, and my works succeeded.
mn39:14.6: I have repaid all the money of the old loan, and there remains over some extra for my wife and children.’
mn39:14.7: And on considering that, he would be glad on that account and find joy on that account.
mn39:14.8: Suppose, bhikkhus, a man was afflicted, suffering and gravely ill, and his food did not sustain him and his body had no strength,
mn39:14.9: but later he recovered from the affliction and his food sustained him and his body regained strength.
mn39:14.10: Then it would occur to him:
mn39:14.11: ‘Formerly I was afflicted, suffering and gravely ill, and my food did not sustain me and my body had no strength; but now I have recovered from that affliction, my food sustains me, and my body has strength.’
mn39:14.12: And on considering that, he would be glad on that account and find joy on that account.
mn39:14.13: Suppose, bhikkhus, a man were imprisoned in a prison-house,
mn39:14.14: but later he was released from that imprisonment, safe and sound, with no loss to his property.
mn39:14.15: Then it would occur to him:
mn39:14.16: ‘Formerly I was imprisoned in a prison-house; but now I am released from that imprisonment, safe and sound, with no loss to my property.’
mn39:14.17: And on considering that, he would be glad on that account and find joy on that account.
mn39:14.18: Suppose, bhikkhus, a man were a bondsman, not self-dependent but dependent on others and unable to go where he wanted,
mn39:14.19: but later on he was released from that bondage, self-dependent, independent of others and a freed man able to go where he wanted.
mn39:14.20: Then it would occur to him:
mn39:14.21: ‘Formerly I was a bondsman, not self-dependent but dependent on others and unable to go where I wanted; but now I am released from that bondage, self-dependent, independent of others and a freed man able to go where I want.’
mn39:14.22: And on considering that, he would be glad on that account and find joy on that account.
mn39:14.23: Suppose, bhikkhus, a man with property and goods entered on a road across a desert,
mn39:14.24: but later on he crossed over the desert, safe and sound, with no loss to his property.
mn39:14.25: Then it would occur to him:
mn39:14.26: ‘Formerly, with property and goods, I entered on a road across a desert.
mn39:14.27: But now I have crossed over that desert, safe and sound, with no loss to my property.’
mn39:14.28: And on considering that, he would be glad on that account and find joy on that account.
mn39:14.29: So too, bhikkhus, when these five hindrances are unabandoned in himself, a bhikkhu sees them respectively as a debt, a disease, a prison-house, a bondage, and a road across a desert.
mn39:14.30: And when these five hindrances are abandoned in himself, he sees that as unindebtedness, healthiness, release from prison, freedom from bondage, and a land of safety.
mn39:15.1: Having abandoned these five hindrances, imperfections of mind that weaken understanding,
mn39:15.2: quite secluded from sensual desires, secluded from unprofitable dhammas, he enters upon and abides in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by initial and sustained application, with happiness and pleasure born of seclusion.
mn39:15.3: He makes happiness and pleasure born of seclusion drench, steep, fill and extend throughout his whole body, so that there is nothing of his whole body to which the happiness and pleasure born of seclusion do not extend.
mn39:15.4: Just as a skilled bath man or bath man’s apprentice heaps bath powder in a metal basin and, sprinkling it gradually with water, kneads it up till the moisture wets his ball of bath powder, soaks it, and extends over it within and without, though it does not itself become liquid;
mn39:15.5: so too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu makes happiness and pleasure born of seclusion drench, steep, fill, and extend throughout this whole body, so that there is nothing of his whole body to which the happiness and pleasure born of seclusion do not extend.
mn39:16.1: Again, with the stilling of initial and sustained application he enters upon and abides in the second jhāna, which has self-confidence and singleness of mind, without initial application and without sustained application, with happiness and pleasure born of concentration.
mn39:16.2: He makes happiness and pleasure born of concentration drench, steep, fill and extend throughout this whole body, and there is nothing of his whole body to which the happiness and pleasure born of concentration do not extend.
mn39:16.3: Just as though there were a lake whose waters welled up from below, having no inflow from east, west, north or south, nor yet replenished from time to time by the skies with showers, then the cool fount of water welling up in the lake would make the cool water drench, steep, fill and extend throughout the lake, and there would be nothing of the whole lake to which the cool water did not extend;
mn39:16.4: so too, bhikkhus, the bhikkhu makes happiness and pleasure born of concentration drench, steep, fill and extend throughout this whole body, so that there is nothing of his whole body to which the happiness and pleasure born of concentration do not extend.
mn39:17.1: Again, with the fading as well of happiness he abides in equanimity, and mindful and fully aware, still feeling pleasure with the body, he enters upon and abides in the third jhāna, on account of which the Noble Ones announce: ‘He has a pleasant abiding who has equanimity and is mindful.’
mn39:17.2: He makes pleasure divested of happiness drench, steep, fill and extend throughout this whole body, and there is nothing of his whole body to which the pleasure divested of happiness does not extend.
mn39:17.3: Just as, in a water-lily pond or a white lotus pond or a red lotus pond, some water-lilies or white lotuses or red lotuses are born under the water, grow under the water, do not stand up out of the water, flourish immersed under the water, and cool water drenches, fills and extends throughout them, to their tips and to their roots, and there is nothing of the whole of those water-lilies, those white lotuses, those red lotuses, to which the cool water does not extend;
mn39:17.4: so too, bhikkhus, the bhikkhu makes pleasure divested of happiness drench, steep, fill and extend throughout this body, and there is nothing of his whole body to which pleasure divested of happiness does not extend.
mn39:18.1: Again, with the abandoning of pleasure and pain, and with the previous disappearance of joy and grief, he enters upon and abides in the fourth jhāna, which has neither-pain-nor-pleasure, and has purity of mindfulness due to equanimity.
mn39:18.2: He sits with a pure bright mind extending over this body, and there is nothing of his whole body to which the pure bright mind does not extend.
mn39:18.3: Just as though a man were sitting clothed from head to foot in white cloth, and there were nothing of his whole body to which the white cloth did not extend;
mn39:18.4: so too, bhikkhus, the bhikkhu sits with a pure bright mind extending over this body, and there is nothing of his whole body to which the pure bright mind does not extend.
mn39:19.1: When the concentrated mind is thus pure and bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, and become malleable, wieldy, steady and attained to imperturbability, he directs, he inclines mind to knowledge of recollection of past life.
mn39:19.2: He recollects his manifold past life … (as in Sutta 4, para. 27) … Thus with details and particulars he recollects his manifold past life.
mn39:19.3: Just as though a man went from his own village to another village, and then he went from that village to another village and then he went back again to his own village, and he thought: ‘I went from my own village to that village, and there such was the way I sat, such the way I spoke, such the way I was silent; and from that village I went to that other village, and there such was the way I stood, such the way I sat, such the way I spoke, such the way I was silent; and from that village I came back again to my own village’;
mn39:19.4: so too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu recollects his manifold past life … Thus with details and particulars he recollects his manifold past life.
mn39:20.1: When the concentrated mind is thus pure and bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, and become malleable, wieldy, steady, and attained to imperturbability, he directs, he inclines, mind to the knowledge of the passing away and reappearance of beings.
mn39:20.2: With the heavenly eyesight, which is purified and surpasses the human, he sees beings passing away and reappearing … (as in Sutta 4, para. 28) …
mn39:20.3: Just as though there were two houses with doors and a man with good eyes standing there in between saw men entering the house and coming out and going to and fro;
mn39:20.4: so too, with heavenly eyesight … He understands how beings pass on according to their kammas.
mn39:21.1: When the concentrated mind is thus pure and bright, unblemished, rid of imperfection, and become malleable, wieldy, steady and attained to imperturbability, he directs, he inclines, mind to the knowledge of the exhaustion of the taints.
mn39:21.2: He understands as it actually is: ‘This is suffering’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the origin of suffering’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the cessation of suffering’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of suffering.’
mn39:21.3: He understands as it actually is: ‘These are the taints’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the origin of the taints’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the cessation of the taints’; he understands as it actually is: ‘This is the way leading to the cessation of the taints.’
mn39:21.4: When he knows and sees thus, his mind is liberated from the taint of sensual desire, from the taint of being, and from the taint of ignorance.
mn39:21.5: When it is liberated there comes the knowledge: ‘It is liberated.’
mn39:21.6: He understands: ‘Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived out, what was to be done is done, there is no more of this to come.’
mn39:21.7: Just as if there were a lake in a mountain recess, clear, limpid and unturbid,
mn39:21.8: so that a man with good eyes standing up there on the bank, saw shells, gravel and pebbles, and also shoals of fish swimming about and resting,
mn39:21.10: ‘There is this lake, clear, limpid and unturbid, and there are these shells, gravel and pebbles, and also these shoals of fish swimming about and resting’;
mn39:21.11: so too, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu understands, as it actually is: ‘This is suffering’ …
mn39:21.12: he understands: ‘there is no more of this to come.’
mn39:22.1: ‘Bhikkhus, it is one such as this who is called a “Monk”, who is called a “Divine”, who is called “Washed”, who is called “Attained to Knowledge”, who is called “In the Stream”, who is called “Noble”, who is called “Arahant”.
mn39:23.1: ‘And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu a “Monk”?
mn39:23.2: He has quieted (samita) evil unprofitable dhammas that defile, renew being, bring misery, ripen as pain, and give future birth, ageing and death.
mn39:23.3: That is how a bhikkhu is a “Monk”.
mn39:24.1: ‘And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu a “Divine”?
mn39:24.2: He has divided himself (bāhita) from evil unprofitable dhammas that defile, renew being, bring misery, ripen as pain, and give future birth, ageing and death.
mn39:24.3: That is how a bhikkhu is a “Divine”.
mn39:25.2: He has washed off evil unprofitable dhammas that defile, renew being, bring misery, ripen as pain, and give future birth, ageing and death.
mn39:25.3: That is how a bhikkhu is “Washed”.
mn39:26.1: ‘And how is a bhikkhu “Attained to Knowledge”?[^3]
mn39:26.2: He has known evil unprofitable dhammas that defile, renew being, bring misery, ripen as pain, and give future birth, ageing and death.
mn39:26.3: That is how a bhikkhu is “Attained to Knowledge”.
mn39:27.1: ‘And how, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu “In the Stream”?
mn39:27.2: He has let the evil unprofitable dhammas that defile, renew being, bring misery, ripen as pain, and give future birth, ageing and death, stream away (nissuta) from him.
mn39:27.3: That is how a bhikkhu is “In the Stream”.
mn39:28.2: Evil unprofitable dhammas that defile, renew being, bring misery, ripen as pain, and give future birth, ageing and death, are far (āraka) from him.
mn39:28.3: That is how a bhikkhu is “Noble”.
mn39:29.2: Evil unprofitable dhammas that defile, renew being, bring misery, ripen as pain, and give future birth, ageing and death, are far from him.
mn39:29.3: That is how a bhikkhu is “Arahant”.’
mn39:29.4: That is what the Blessed One said.
mn39:29.5: The bhikkhus were satisfied, and they delighted in the Blessed One’s words.
